title: Uniform Acceleration Kinematics & v–t Graphs
theory: Constant acceleration $a$ means the v–t graph is a straight line of slope $a$; **displacement = area under the v–t curve**; the average velocity over any interval is $(v_i+v_f)/2$. When a problem says "accelerates uniformly from rest to $v$ in time $t$", draw the triangle — the answer is its area.

formulas.description: [$v$: speed, m/s; $a$: acceleration, m/s²; $t$: time, s]

framework: Choose the kinematic equation that omits the variable you neither know nor need.
For graphs: slope = acceleration, area = displacement.

parts.parameters:
- Given: car starts from rest, reaches speed $v$ after time $t$, uniform acceleration.
- Find: distance traveled during $t$.
- Diagram: v–t graph = right triangle, base $t$, height $v$.
parts.conclusion: One line via the area — $a$ is never needed. Trap (a) $vt$ assumes constant speed; sanity: with acceleration from rest the distance must be *less* than $vt$. A 20-second problem — bank the time.
